The sources disagree widely, mostly because they measure different things: the tokenizer used, the text type, and whether the comparison is a true translation or a literal string.

**Measurements using o200k_base**

- **About 1.3–1.4x English.** A blog author tokenized 285 posts, each published in Korean and English, and found Korean ran 1.38x English tokens, Japanese 1.34x. A separate study of 8 meaning-matched pairs found the mean ratio was 1.30x (median 1.33x, range 1.09x to 1.42x). That study also found technical paragraphs were worst at 1.42x. The sample is small, so treat it as indicative.
- **A single example.** One author's sentence came out at twelve tokens under OpenAI's o200k_base in English and twenty tokens in Korean, about 1.7x for that sentence.

**Higher ratios reported**

- One author who translated a blog post reported that translating a 1,500-word English blog post into Korean consumed 2.8x more tokens than the English source. The tokenizer is not named in that excerpt, so it may not be o200k_base. Translation style may also account for part of the gap.
- A Korean academic paper (ICICPE 2024) reports that tokenization of the Korean sentence resulted in nearly four times more tokens. That paper used GPT-4's tokenizer, which is cl100k_base, not o200k_base. It also used the FLORES200 parallel corpus, so its ratio is not directly comparable to the o200k figures above.

**Why the ratio varies**

Two contributing factors are cited. One is training data: Major LLM training corpora are 1–3% Korean, meaning few dedicated Korean tokens enter the vocabulary. The other is byte-level fallback, where out-of-vocabulary characters fall back to UTF-8 byte-level splitting, so a single character can become 2–3 tokens.

**Older tokenizer comparison**

The o200k_base tokenizer is generally reported to be more efficient for Korean than cl100k_base. One forum post notes that it has a very deep alphabet, generally one token per Hangul character for the 100k tokenizer, which suggests that the older tokenizer is not uniformly worse. The results I found do not directly compare the two on identical Korean text, so I cannot give a precise cl100k-to-o200k ratio for Korean.

**Bottom line:** For o200k_base, the best-supported range is roughly **1.3–1.4x** English tokens for meaning-matched text. Some translated long-form content measured higher, up to about 2.8x, though it is not clear the tokenizer was o200k_base. Measure your own text with `tiktoken.get_encoding('o200k_base')` before relying on any single figure.

I found no official Anthropic figure for this. The published numbers come from third-party measurements, and they range from roughly 1.3x to 3x depending on method.

- **About 1.3x to 1.4x (same meaning):** One blogger measured eight Korean/English sentence pairs with OpenAI's o200k_base tokenizer, not Claude's, and got a mean ratio of about 1.3x. The mean ratio was 1.30x (median 1.33x, range 1.09x to 1.42x). A separate analysis of 285 articles reports that Korean costs 1.4x English, and it counted Claude tokens using the community-maintained Xenova/claude-tokenizer on Hugging Face.
- **Higher, per-character view:** A third-party cost comparison says on Claude, Chinese runs about 114 net tokens per 100 characters, Korean 106, Japanese 94, against 32 for English. Per-character counts overstate the gap, because Korean characters carry more meaning per character than English letters. The same post warns that read that column alone and CJK looks like a 3x tax.
- **Higher, anecdotal:** A user feature request on Claude Code's GitHub-style tracker estimates that the same meaning expressed in Korean requires approximately 1.5x to 3x more tokens than English. Its examples are approximate and not a controlled test.

Caveats:
- Anthropic does not publish its tokenizer, so every Claude count here comes from an unofficial approximation or from API token counts. Treat the figures as estimates.
- The methods differ. Some use parallel sentences, some use whole articles, and some use per-character counts. Only the first two give a true "same content" ratio.
- Tokenizers differ across model families. One source notes that Claude Fable 5, Opus 4.8, and Sonnet 5 share one tokenizer, but it does not give a Korean-specific ratio for those models.
- For your own numbers, run the same Korean and English text through the token-counting endpoint in Anthropic's API or the current official tokenizer tool.

The paper is "Language Model Tokenizers Introduce Unfairness Between Languages" by Aleksandar Petrov, Emanuele La Malfa, Philip Torr, and Adel Bibi. It was published at NeurIPS 2023. However, I couldn't find any result that specifically reports a Korean tokenization premium, so I can't confirm what the paper says about Korean.

**What the paper covers**
- The authors argue that language inequality begins at tokenization, before a model runs. The same text translated into different languages can have drastically different tokenization lengths, with differences up to 15 times in some cases.
- The gap persists across tokenizers. The arXiv version says that across 17 tokenizers that power popular language models such as ChatGPT and GPT-4, regardless whether they use a word, subword, character, or byte-level tokenization, there always exists disadvantaged languages that are at least 4 times less efficient than others.
- The paper ties these differences to three harms. One is cost, since commercial services charge users per token or Unicode character. Another is latency, since the number of tokens has a direct effect on the processing time for a task. The third concerns how much content fits into a model's context window.
- The authors conclude that we should train future language models using multilingually fair subword tokenizers.

**Version differences**
The paper's text and abstracts vary slightly. One text version says that these discrepancies lead to users of some languages paying at least 2.5 times more for the same task as users of English. The arXiv version says at least 4 times. Check the specific version you're citing.

**Korean specifically**
Neither search surfaced Korean-specific figures from the paper. If you need them, the full PDF or the GitHub repository (github.com/AleksandarPetrov/tokenization-fairness) includes per-language tokenization length tables, and Korean would be listed there. Separately, a 2025 paper on Korean tokenization, Thunder-Tok, addresses token fertility for Korean specifically, which may be relevant to your question. It introduces Thunder-Tok, a new Korean tokenizer designed to reduce token fertility without compromising model performance.

content.text:
No hay una cifra única ni oficial. Según los estudios que encontré, el coreano usa **entre 1,3 y 1,4 veces más tokens** que el inglés con los tokenizadores actuales, comparando textos que dicen lo mismo. En casos concretos la diferencia puede llegar a 2–4 veces.

## OpenAI

| Tokenizador | Coreano vs. inglés | Fuente |
|---|---|---|
| **o200k_base** (GPT‑4o y posteriores) | **1,38×** (285 artículos publicados en ambos idiomas) | [jangwook.net](https://jangwook.net/en/blog/en/multilingual-llm-token-tax-experiment/) |
| o200k_base | **1,30×** de media (mediana 1,33×, rango 1,09–1,42×; 8 pares de frases con el mismo significado; los párrafos técnicos salen peor) | [DEV Community](https://dev.to/claudeguide/korean-vs-english-do-you-pay-more-tokens-for-the-same-prompt-jm8) |
| o200k_base | ~1,7× en una sola frase de ejemplo (12 tokens frente a 20) | [DEV Community](https://dev.to/claudeguide/korean-vs-english-do-you-pay-more-tokens-for-the-same-prompt-jm8) |
| **cl100k_base** (GPT‑4, GPT‑3.5) | Hasta **~4×** en frases del corpus paralelo FLORES‑200 | [Korea University, ICICPE 2024](https://hiai.korea.ac.kr/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/Korean-Penalty-of-Large-Language-Models-Derived-by-the-Tokenizer_ICICPE_2024.pdf) |

Se suele decir que o200k_base trata el coreano mejor que cl100k_base, pero no encontré ninguna medición que compare los dos con el mismo texto coreano.

## Claude (Anthropic)

Anthropic no publica su tokenizador actual, así que estas cifras son estimaciones de terceros:

- **~1,4×**: el mismo estudio de 285 artículos ([jangwook.net](https://jangwook.net/en/blog/en/multilingual-llm-token-tax-experiment/)). Usó `Xenova/claude-tokenizer`, una versión de la comunidad publicada en Hugging Face. Hasta donde sé, corresponde al tokenizador de los modelos Claude antiguos, por lo que puede no reflejar los modelos actuales.
- **Contando por caracteres**: ~106 tokens por cada 100 caracteres en coreano frente a ~32 en inglés ([DEV Community – synthorai](https://dev.to/synthorai/which-llm-is-cheapest-for-your-language-tokenizer-costs-measured-1k5m)). Esto parece una diferencia de unas 3 veces, pero exagera el problema: un carácter coreano lleva mucha más información que una letra inglesa. El propio autor lo advierte.
- **1,5–3×**: estimación aproximada, sin pruebas controladas, de un usuario en una petición de mejora de Claude Code ([claudeissues.com #26401](https://claudeissues.com/issue/26401-feature-request-non-english-users-korean-japanese-cjk-face-structural-disadvanta)).

## Por qué ocurre

- **Datos de entrenamiento:** el coreano es solo un 1–3 % de los corpus con que se entrenan los modelos. Por eso hay pocos tokens dedicados al coreano en el vocabulario.
- **Caracteres desconocidos:** cuando un carácter no está en el vocabulario, se divide en bytes UTF‑8, y una sola sílaba hangul puede acabar en 2–3 tokens ([jangwook.net](https://jangwook.net/en/blog/en/multilingual-llm-token-tax-experiment/)).
- **Contexto general:** Petrov et al. (NeurIPS 2023) analizaron 17 tokenizadores. Entre idiomas encontraron diferencias de longitud de hasta 15 veces, y siempre hay idiomas al menos 4 veces menos eficientes que otros ([NeurIPS](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2023/hash/74bb24dca8334adce292883b4b651eda-Abstract.html), [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.15425v1)). En lo que encontré no aparece una cifra específica para el coreano. La tabla por idiomas está en su [repositorio de GitHub](https://github.com/AleksandarPetrov/tokenization-fairness).

## Advertencias

- Casi todas las fuentes son blogs con muestras pequeñas. El único estudio académico usa el tokenizador antiguo de OpenAI (cl100k_base).
- El resultado cambia mucho según el método: frases con el mismo significado (1,3–1,4×), conteo por caracteres (~3×) o traducciones libres (una entrada de blog habla de 2,8×).
- Para tener cifras fiables con tu propio texto, mídelo directamente. Para OpenAI, con `tiktoken.get_encoding("o200k_base")`. Para Claude, con el endpoint `count_tokens` de la API de Anthropic, que usa el tokenizador real del modelo. Si quieres, preparo un script que compare ambos con tus textos.

- **Contando por caracteres**: ~106 tokens por cada 100 caracteres en coreano frente a ~32 en inglés ([DEV Community – synthorai](https://dev.to/synthorai/which-llm-is-cheapest-for-your-language-tokenizer-costs-measured-1k5m)). Esto parece una diferencia de unas 3 veces, pero exagera el problema: un carácter coreano lleva mucha más información que una letra inglesa. El propio autor lo advierte.
- **1,5–3×**: estimación aproximada, sin pruebas controladas, de un usuario en una petición de mejora de Claude Code ([claudeissues.com #26401](https://claudeissues.com/issue/26401-feature-request-non-english-users-korean-japanese-cjk-face-structural-disadvanta)).

## Por qué ocurre

- **Datos de entrenamiento:** el coreano es solo un 1–3 % de los corpus con que se entrenan los modelos. Por eso hay pocos tokens dedicados al coreano en el vocabulario.
- **Caracteres desconocidos:** cuando un carácter no está en el vocabulario, se divide en bytes UTF‑8, y una sola sílaba hangul puede acabar en 2–3 tokens ([jangwook.net](https://jangwook.net/en/blog/en/multilingual-llm-token-tax-experiment/)).
- **Contexto general:** Petrov et al. (NeurIPS 2023) analizaron 17 tokenizadores. Entre idiomas encontraron diferencias de longitud de hasta 15 veces, y siempre hay idiomas al menos 4 veces menos eficientes que otros ([NeurIPS](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2023/hash/74bb24dca8334adce292883b4b651eda-Abstract.html), [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.15425v1)). En lo que encontré no aparece una cifra específica para el coreano. La tabla por idiomas está en su [repositorio de GitHub](https://github.com/AleksandarPetrov/tokenization-fairness).

## Advertencias

- Casi todas las fuentes son blogs con muestras pequeñas. El único estudio académico usa el tokenizador antiguo de OpenAI (cl100k_base).
- El resultado cambia mucho según el método: frases con el mismo significado (1,3–1,4×), conteo por caracteres (~3×) o traducciones libres (una entrada de blog habla de 2,8×).
- Para tener cifras fiables con tu propio texto, mídelo directamente. Para OpenAI, con `tiktoken.get_encoding("o200k_base")`. Para Claude, con el endpoint `count_tokens` de la API de Anthropic, que usa el tokenizador real del modelo. Si quieres, preparo un script que compare ambos con tus textos.
